To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
blue-cone monochrome (BCM) is the result of a mutation in the tandem array that encodes the visual pigments of the red and green cones.

the tandem array of red- and green-pigment genes is rearranged in blue-cone monochrome subjects, that these rearrangements are associated with a Cys203-to-Tyr mutation in the blue pigment gene in some subjects, and that there is a reservoir of chromosomes with the Cys203-to-Ary mutation that can generate blue-cone monchromacy by unequal homologus recombination and/or point mutation.
blue-cone monochrome is caused by a number of different mutations in the red and green pigment genes and that the mutations are not all the same.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic basis of blue-cone color deficiency.
the genetic and biochemical basis of human color vision.
the genetic and biochemical mechanisms that lead to blue cone monochromacy and other forms of congenital color-vision deficiency.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
blue-cone monochrome is a heterogeneous condition with at least four genotypic classes.
there is no single genetic cause of blue-cone-monochrome.
blue-cone monochrome is the end result of a number of different mutational events, each of which is rare, but each of which can be identified.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

there are at least 12 different genotypes that can produce blue-cone monochrome phenotypes, and that there are at leat 5 different mutational mechanisms that can generate blue-cone monosomy genotypes.
there are at least 10 different genotypes that can give rise to the clinical syndrome of blue-cone-monochrome.

the blue-cone-monochrome genotypes are generated by the same mechanisms of gene rearrangement that are responsible for generating the normal red/green polymorphism, with the addition of a Cys203-to-Tyr mutation that predisposes the red/green pigment genes to gene conversion and unequal crossing-over.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is considerable heterogeneity of genotype in blue-cone-monochrome subjects, which is consistent with the idea that there are multiple mutational pathways to the disease.
there are multiple pathways to the loss of red and green cone function in blue cone monochromats.
there is a great deal of heterogeneity in the molecular basis of blue cone monochromacy, and that there may be multiple pathways that lead to this phenotype.
